blocks.x: Why don't we get your right name?
Well, actually my name is E.T. Kelly. And I acquired the Tim because my dad told me that was what the T in my name is. It means to be E Timothy Kelly.
And you never tell anybody what the E stands for?
Edward. Edward, right. Very straightforward.
And where are we?
Well, where are we?
Now, what's the address?
We're at 455 Roxbury Road in Jackson, Mississippi. And we're with Mr. Howard Jones, one of my favorite trombone players, and Mr. Dick Hammond.
I work in the library there. I don't know if I told you, but we have a big collection there. Including Jack Teagarden talking about you on the stage.
Oh, well, that's nice. I had no idea of that.

Well, Jack is one of the first people I think who ever told me. Anyway, today is December the... Third? The third, 1978. And this is your home, of course. Just to ask you some standard questions, when were you born and where?

Dick, I was born in Mississippi. Born out in the country from Meridian in 1905. I was living out there. My family was living in Marshall, Texas, where I was actually here. Okay. But I actually was born in Lauderdale County, Mississippi.
The exact date?
July 25, 1905. My mother was such a Mississippian that she just wanted me to be born over here. So, they came over from Texas, so I could be born in Mississippi.
And they had moved over there, I guess?

Yeah, my father was with the Tex-Pacific Railroad, and he had gone over there, and they had been living in Marshall for several years. I have two sisters, Sister Mary and Sister Mary. They were both older than I. And so, I often say I was made in Texas and born in Mississippi.
And were they musicals at Browning?

Well, my two sisters both played piano, but they just studied it and played, you know, very well. All girls at that time were supposed to take piano, so they did. I had one great uncle who was a country fiddler, and then as far as my Irish ancestors were playing, they were musical people too. Nobody in the family we knew. Nobody in the family we knew particularly musical.
They did play well. Do you remember the names of any of them?

Well, the country fiddler was my Uncle Gus Clayton. And he was a Mississippi and played four dances out in the country, you know, just like those square dances and things like that. My father was often worried. He'd say, there you go. You're going to be like Uncle Gus, playing that music. They were not particularly interested in having me play, but my sisters were all far and my mother died when I was very young. And I became interested in playing. We had a school, East End School band in Marshall. And I had been listening to records, Art Hickman, original Dixeland Jazz Band, Louisiana, and other, Old Wilber C. Sweatman, different recordings. We didn't have a patrol, but the neighbors across the street had one, had a wonderful selection record. So I just became interested in it that way. And it started very young. And I played, actually, ordered a clarinet from Charlie Parker in Houston, the band director that came out in the barns park, even in those days. In fact, the little towns didn't have the music stuff to an extent. They had to be ordered from Houston or Dallas. And so, the day I got my clarinet, one of the neighbor boys, Harold Atkins, already played the clarinet. He came by the house and showed me the fingering and I could play the clarinet. And I started like that.
Did you have, could you play by ear or were you?

Yeah. He showed me the fingering and I could play immediately because I had, of course I had played on the king flutes and which is similar to our modern fluter fans. So, I just was kind of extremely interested from the beginning.
Well, since you know so much about instruments, I assume, you're in the business. What kind of clarinet was it? Do you have any idea?

Well, the first clarinet, and I think this is an interesting story. I've told him a lot of times, but it's true. The band director came around to the kids and said, I can get you an Albert System clarinet for $36. I can get you an Albert System clarinet, that's the new kind, for $80. And I had the $36 and I didn't have the $80, so I didn't know the difference. I took the Albert and I've always played the same thing. But the name of the clarinet, the first one I ever had was a Henry Gunkel. G-U-N-K-E-L, which came from Charlie Park in Houston. It was just one of any number of names which were used on clarinet. The distributors only put a name on most of them. For their cheap instruments, they'll use a local name, just like Whirlines, very often have stenciled instruments under their own name, the band for the New York Clans.
So it was a fairly simple thing, fairly close to the can read.

Albert System clarinet is, of course, it's different from the band system clarinet, in that the band is an improved fingering mechanism. But, Albert is, I don't know, he just seemed to fall into it naturally. Easier to play by here, anybody who has, you'd say a little knack for it. But, I left home, actually, I became interested in playing, we had a little jazz band there in town. They had a band called Tim Shrill, not needed, but Tim Atkins. And, in this group, they had a Jewish drummer, Jake Goldberg, had a tenor saxophone player whose name was Carl Limburg, and Tim Atkins, an Englishman, was a pianist and leader. So, all the kids were excited about it. They were playing dances and making them, and they were a little bit older than our group. But, there was another little small group in town, and called the Melody Corps. And, they got a job that needed a saxophone player, and I didn't have a saxophone player. They said, you teach, you get a pair of long pants, then you get a C Melody Sax, we'll give you a job. So, I borrowed the sax, and they got me some long pants, and then we played Carthage, Texas, which is very close to Marshall's. And, we were $12.50 for our evening. And, that ended my delivering packages for the grocery store, drug store, and other places, because that seemed like an awful lot of money just to play three hours. So, from then on out, I continued to listen to other people who were better. And, before long, they started asking me to come up to Terrell, Texas, and Minniova, which are on the Dallas from Marshall. And, I had a pass on the Sunshine Special.
Oh.

So, on Friday nights, I would go up and play with these little bands. Well, of course, I knew that I was going to play in a band. That's all I was going to say. I just had to do that. And, so, pretty soon, I just, without my father's permission, I just left and joined this little band. And, we went to Terrell, Texas, and played in a cafe. And, then we played nights in Athens and all the little Texas towns around 50 mile radius. And, this was really before I ever got out on the road to play with other territory of bands. But, we, I just, I often left. And, my father was very kind. And, instead of putting me on a reform school or something, my sister talked him out of being real bad to him. And, she said, well, I came back on, after this little incident. And, I guess I stayed maybe, went on to school, stayed for some months. And, then, Ham Crawford's band, which was said to be from Havana, Cuba. They'd been playing through East Texas, and they were extremely popular. And, Ham was really a very good saxophonist and had good musicians working there. So, he was one of the largest bands. So, they had three of us, a trio. So, he said, we're going to enlarge the band for six pieces and move another sax and playing that. So, I joined the band, again, without the permission of my folks. But, I just felt I had to do it, to me.
How old was it?
I was sixteen.
Where was Ham Crawford's son?

Ham Crawford was actually from Tyler, Texas. I thought he had been. And, Dick, he had been playing with an orchestra in Dallas, which was very famous in those days, called the Jack Gardner Orchestra. And, so he'd been there a couple times to march to play with this other band. This goes very thankful. The Jack Gardner band was most popular in Texas, all of Texas, and they were in great demand. They rode the Pullman. They all wore the same beautiful suits. You know, not uniforms, but business suits. They traveled in great style. And, of course, kids, we'd go to the ballroom where they played, Holly's Hall. And, I have a good friend who managed to dance with me, let me know. So, I would get to hear them, and that's where I first heard him. But, he is famous for going around in different territories and getting bands, getting young guys who were good, and then taking them on the road.
He did Winging one time.
Sure did.
I don't know how long Winging lasted, did he?
Well, Winging, yeah. Winging joined him in Albuquerque, New Mexico. And, well, no, I'm not so sure about that. Winging joined Doc Ross Band in Albuquerque.
I think there was some of those mix-ups there. But, I think, I believe I got this story from Jack, or from the book about Jack D.

Well, Winging is one of my oldest friends. And, we didn't play together until the thirties. But, we'd been friends. He had come through school for two or three times. And, after playing with him, that is how the original Buddy's Three Melody Boys came about. The Buddy's were part of him for the band. And, him decided he wanted to have a number two band. So, he got a job in Monroe. After he washed off his Daryl roof. The Washedaw Bank roof. That's where he was. One of the first roof columns and he was part of the country school. I can stop.
Maybe Howard's chunking rocks with that bone. Well, I checked it. Oh, okay.
Well, I guess maybe it would be, uh.
We're talking about the number two band. Yeah.

So, uh. Ham sent us to Lake Charles, which is where I heard some early little bands we used to play. Big Lake and we played Shaw Beach, Pleasure Field. At that time, it was a real nice resort out in the lake. That was before Lake Charles became the Dakota Port. And, we were swimming and then we had a ballroom out over the world. And, it was real nice. We're talking about 1923 now. And, um. So, after leaving Lake Charles, this group of fellas, Brooks Prud and Dick Coleman and Buddy Seabee and myself, went back to Shreveport and organized the Buddies Blue Melody Boys. Buddies Blue Melody Boys was the group that I was identified with for most of the several years that I first played. And, it was a very good band of the time. Some of the best musicians would, of course, would go through this band. We had the same personnel, but sometimes we played together as long as two years without single change. We all had all head arrangements. We, uh. We were really together and had a great time. Played all through North Texas, East Texas, New Cork, Mississippi, Arkansas. And, we did this in the Ford automobile. At first, with ice and glass curtains, we packed up, sometimes six guys, strap all of the stuff on the back of the Ford. And, we were booked. There was an interesting thing. We were booked by a man named Jasper Tompkins. We were booked, oh, dozens of names. Black names they had white names they had. And, first time Jack Teagarden played in Shreveport, he played for Jasper Tompkins. Played with Terry Sheehan and Reginald Gullick. They had a trio.
Reginald who?

Gullick. And, Thomas Joyner. Now, these are names you may not be familiar with, but they're well-known, well-well-known at this time. But, Jack was the outstanding star. Is that the same as Tommy Joyner?
Tommy Joyner.
Is his name as Tallis? Yeah. What did you call him? Tommy?
Tommy, uh-huh. And, he played, that's the drummer on Zalifon.
Yeah, that's right. I've heard of him. He's from Tyler, Texas, too, sir.
Oh, I see. And, uh... And, the other man you mentioned before him, there's Terry Sheehan and somebody in between.
Oh.
I didn't get what he played. Well, actually, this was just a little trio.

And, it was Jack and Terry Sheehan up in, uh, Thomas John, and William Gramsson, and all that stuff. And, they played all the society dances, and they played the Fiori roof garden. And, this particular man, this guy, who I was talking about, uh, was, uh, Asian. He hired them. And, uh, so I guess the buddies then, uh, who, uh, who, uh, were, uh, uh, who, uh, were included the Red Round Tree and Buddy Seeky and drums and, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, who included Red Roundtree and Buddy Seaton on drums and Shockey Wilcox on trumpet. And Red Roundtree was a very famous banjo player who played with Lute Speed, and he was at the Arcade Studios in California for 20 years, and he's still living. And I had recently been out to see him and jammed with me at all. So the Buddies then, after the Buddies broke up, I had several offers to join different bands. So I went to Houston for a little while and played at what's called Basho Park. And I always kicked myself because Jack and Peck were playing with Galveston, which was not more than 50 miles away than they would get together. At that time. But so much of my history ties in with Snoozer and Jack and Peck, although I didn't work with Peck, but I was first years. And he came up the street to it. So after I went to Houston, I went out to Wichita Falls, Texas, and played with the 80s trumpeters. And there were some real fine musicians in there, Sam Bird, Ridge Stewart, Aida Whitley. I can't remember the trumpet players, but they had done that. Anyway, I just had all these offers. Everything was done by telegram. The guys, they'd wire you and say, have a nice job, $60 a week or $50 a week or whatever. Must have done that. So I decided to take several of those jobs, and I did. And I just stayed for maybe six weeks, two months, and I'd go. Always end up back in the street with the Buddies from the other, but they'd always continued to me. Now, I'll get into some things I think would be more interesting to. The Louisiana Rounders were organized by Pat and Bob DeQueer, who were from New Iberia. And they originally called themselves the original Jazzland Six. And in the twenties, they played all over Southern Louisiana. They were the earliest white musicians I ever heard who really played black. I mean, in the exact style of Southern Louisiana black musicians. They were tremendous. But we didn't realize how good they worked until late years. And so, they actually came to El Dorado, Arkansas, and played in the oil fields for just a short time. And then they came over to Shreveport and organized the Louisiana Rambles. Well, this was under a piano player named Bob Canfield, but it was a kind of a band that all the people shared in, and they were all that's familiar. And they developed into, in my idea, the best big band that we ever had in that part of the country. They had Bert Sigerson from New Orleans, a name you may not be at all familiar with, a great tenor saxophone player, still living as far as I know, and lived in New Orleans. And, Pat and Bob, Pat played trumpet, Bob played trumpet, Bob. They had a wonderful drummer named Norm Landry. Norm is now still living and playing in Houston, Texas. And Pat and Bob were both there. Bob Canfield was there. But anyway, they had always wanted me to join them. I preferred to play one-nighters on the roads in small towns and another half-clun. But they finally taught me into joining the band, because I did after the Hotel Washington in Shreveport. And that was some of the best chords I ever did, if I think it was good, worth the round of the chords. But we had over a hundred arrangements committed to memory. We could just knock them off, you know. Nobody had any music. And, but we had hard arrangements and played them well. So, I went on from the Ramblers after they broke up. I went out to California and played, but that's when I first played with Jack. I had met him in Shreveport and we became fast friends. But he was with Doc Ross' band out in Los Angeles. So, he wired for me to come. I drove 2,000 miles out to play with Jack. Two Doc Ross' jazz bandits. But, I had married in the meantime. And, I had to stay in California for a short time. Claiborne Bryson was organizing a band to open at the Jure Hotel that spring. And, he had most of the old ramblers with him. And, so, he called me and cried and he wanted to come back to me for his kid. And, this takes us up to about 1926. And, well, there was a music store opening in the street for Okahop Music Fund. It was referring very much like Werleim's. They had a cool store chain. They were very good people. And, I had decided then that I couldn't be very happy to marry me on the road. And, music business is best is always a hard way to make a living. So, I decided I wanted to go in the music store. I'd been hanging around the music stores from the time I was 13, 14 years old. In the hometown. They would let me talk and do a little bit chores. And, the drummer with the little bands that were playing locally was the chief salesman for this company. So, I just went into the music stores. And, I guess that was when I was like, and I went back to playing a number of different times. And, I played weekends for 20 years with various combinations. Always generally in the open city and which store, wherever. We were always the best union bands. Strictly union. And, of course, had the pleasure of jamming with incoming musicians. And, Dick, I'm kind of, actually kind of a historian of jazz myself. It's a hobby with me. And, I just always kept up with it, like some guys do baseball and other things these times. And, I might not have been able to tell you who was president that year, but I could tell you who played Cristalpa as Duke Ellington. That type of thing. So, it's just always been a wonderful, fascinating thing for me. And, I've continued it. I had a good pleasure to play with people like, started with people like Jack and Winnie. Dan Flossman was one of my real first friends. And, we played together in the school court in 1943. And, it's a long, I could burn for hours. But, I just, it's just been always fun for me. And, I've kept it up a little bit. Maybe I sneak five minutes in the office or at home. I don't get to practice any length of time, because there's always something else to do, you know, like these guitars or whatever. But, I always managed to keep it up enough where I could play the Tin Roof Blues pretty good with Howard. Is that right, Hal?
No, that's right. You didn't tell me much about New Orleans, you tripped down.
Okay. Let me turn this machine over here for a second.
Just so I can see what's happening here. I'm trying to figure out how to prop it out. That's okay. Go ahead. It's facing you.

Okay. There was a music store in 3-4th, formed by Bubba Broyles. Bubba was a trumpet player, and he'd been playing with the local bands there. And, he was a great friend of Mr. A.J. LaCoste, who was a power with the Whirland Organization. A.J. was the management of the band department. He organized school bands all over Mississippi and Louisiana. He was a tremendous man. But, Bubba and LaCoste asked me to come to New Orleans, that I would have some kind of a job. I had, I tried to go back to playing and played with Dick Richardson's band out of Dallas and played with numerous bands, but there wasn't any work. I guess it was in 1930, the bottom. Well, I didn't even tell you if I found my own band. I took a wonderful band out on the road in 1930. Of all times, we would take a band on the road. I took them out in 1930. And, among them were some of the classical musicians in the whole country. And, so, let's see, where have we found here? Well, anyway, my little band had broken up. And, I was supposed to go to work for a group in Shreveport who were playing at the radio station. Well, when I got over there, there was a young kid playing the old fellow who was working his way through school. And, he was a good saxophone player. And, so, I didn't want to bump him up. The guys that asked me to come over, but when I got there, it didn't seem a comfortable thing to do. So, there I was, but I ate jobs. So, I was hanging around Bubba's music store. He said, I'll get you a job in New Orleans. So, I went on to New Orleans in 1932. And, that is the year that the Ben Pollack Band played Club Forrest in New Orleans. And, Aidy Miller had just joined the band. And, of course, Jack G. Gardner and all of the, what later became the Fosby Band. They were Prince Preet. Stirling Bowles was with them. Jack was with them. Matt and Matt Rock was with them. Ray Badoop was with them. Natty Lamar was with them. All of these guys. And, I went out to hear them. And, it was great. And, I'll never forget that the night that I was there, we went to the Studio Club. At that time, there were just two clubs on Bourbon Street. One was the Studio Club and one was the Silver Slipper. Sharky was playing Silver Slipper and had a little band at the Studio Club with Pat De Queer. And, that was where I posed in and numerous other guys. Bob Fryberger, who you probably have never heard of, but he was a Yankee. Great Trombone player who was there. And, so, on that trip, I had an interview with Mr. McCausse. Mr. McCausse said, okay, come on down. I'll put you on a commission basis. And, you can play on the side of the mic. So, I came back to the Streetport and I had a little Pontiac, a Port Caballet.
You have to be careful. Now you were talking about Leslie Nurse, was his name?

Yeah. Leslie and Bill Nurse were two brothers. One played piano and one played banjo. They had a little band in the street, but their parents had moved to New Orleans. My father was a Presbyterian minister, and so Leslie and I drove down to New Orleans, and Johnny Grant, who was a drummer from Straitford, had a room at 327 Bourbon Street. It was a rooming house. He offered me an opportunity to stay with him. I didn't have to pay any of that. I landed in New Orleans for eight dollars, and I planned that in the Satchelor in the province of the Johnwood, where I went. And so, Johnny was in, though. He'd been playing with other bands all around town.
That's with the Owls at one time, I remember. Sure.

Could be wrong, could have been. Johnny possibly played with everybody in the room. Any number of bands, because he lived down there for a long period. He finally went to California. So Johnny, of course, helped me. I worked at Warlands. I got to meet all these musicians around New Orleans. All the jobs were booked down in front of Warlands. They weren't booked at the Union or any place. I was booked in front of Warlands. In fact, police used to have to make the guys, they would be so thick, in front of 605, Canal Street. The cops would very often say, move on, move on. Customers can't get in there. But anyway, these guys would book spot jobs. And that's when I got started. They would come up to the counter and I was, they knew I played. You got a job Friday night? I said, no, I don't like a job. Okay, I want you. So, I really got lots of jobs. I played with little non-union bands like Gimelli, Joe Gimelli, I don't know if you know, I'm Angelo Gimelli, and played a lot with Pete B. Lesseps, who was a very successful agent and an orchestra leader in the Warlands. We worked in the bank. All these guys were, they were sidelining people too. But we played lots of jobs. I remember one time playing a job over at the St. Charles, which was called the President's of the National League of the War. I don't know if you've heard of this before, but at that time, during the Depression, bands would invite all of the presidents of the various social clubs to a dance. And even these two or three bands who went in on it would pay for the expense of the ballroom, refreshments, and everything, so that they had an opportunity to show how they could play and book dates. Now this is something in New Orleans history, I don't know if you've been told, but it was
absolutely an absolute fact.
No, I've never heard of this. President's Ball.
President's Ball.

I mean, the presence of fraternities, carnival clubs, and various other organizations, and it would be quite a big thing. And so they got a lot of this engagement, and they sounded like it. So I played, I actually played with over 200 different New Orleans musicians, and I had the names of practically all of them. I just remembered them through the years, and I wrote them down after I left down there, because I knew I liked them and had so much fun with them. But when my fortunes improved, after a while, one of the fellows who was assistant manager of the department, got in some trouble with the company, and so they had to let him go. And so Mr. LaCrosse made me assistant manager of the department. And then I went on a salary, which was $25 a week and 2% of sales. Now remember, this is 1932, when I could go directly across the street from 327 Brooklyn and get a wonderful meal for 15 cents. That's actually cool.
What was the name of the restaurant?

I can't remember, but it was just almost directly across the street. It was in the 327, close to where the Royal Semester is now. And I lived at the Pontaubo building as soon as I got a salary, and had another close friend at Royal Arms who was in the refrigerator department, the name was Bennett D's. And then I shared 519, we lived at 519 St. Henn, first floor apartment, $45 a month. He paid $22.50 and I paid $22.50. And he was a great bathtub gin mixer, and we had lots of fun. Snoozer used to come down and play for me. We'd, we had a deck chair, had a little banana tree, it was really, it had some fine atmosphere. And Snoozer would play just as long as we'd hand him a drink. He'd just play for me. Sidney Ayrton, the guy who wrote Lazy River, used to come down. Cause they all liked to come down. They didn't have access to, to those things too much. And we were really living just fine. I'd get up in the morning and just walk straight up the street to the Royal Arms, you know, enter on the back side, on the Charlotte Street side, and go to work. And, and just a few blocks home, you know, no traffic problem, no nothing. Just, I enjoyed it very much. But, all good things have to come to their name sometimes. So, uh, Elmo Gogeti, who is 45, was with Werleins, 45 years, had been running Collins Pianicone, which was actually owned by Werleins, and under a different name. And so, they closed them up. And so, Gogeti, they had to make a place for Gogeti. So, uh, they brought Gogeti over and gave him the job I had, and put me back on a straight permission arrangement. And by this time, I was about ready to go back playing anyway. So, I had an offer to go to Beaumont and play with Pat and Bob Dequeer. And in a band called the New Orleans. And, uh, and from there, I played about a year that time, I guess. And, uh, after that, I went on, that's when I went back to Strayport, and, uh, to join. And, uh, it's a Dick Richardson band, really. But, Dean Kincaid was the arranger. Yank Lawson was one of the trumpeters. Wenge was one of the trumpeters. Roger Boyd, who is one of the really great drummers. He's dead now, he was one of them. In fact, this band was terrific. It was just wonderful. We rehearsed all day long. We had boom syringes, which were very modern at that time. And, uh, so, we were supposed to open at a new nightclub in Strayport, called The Castle. But, they, the man who actually had the hiring of the band, had charged the hiring of the band, was Paul English. Paul English was a famous, tense show man. He had had, uh, wonderful dramatic stock companies, and, uh, traveled all over Louisiana. This was a popular thing, they did dramatic shows at that time. But, he was a showman all the way through. So, we were sitting there, starving, and rehearsing, and waiting to go into the castle. He went to Kansas City, and he heard a band called the Taurus Brothers. They had three changes of uniform. They played all kinds of Latin music, and, uh, just a show band out of the world. So, he came back, said, boys, I'm real soft. But, I just had to hire the first time. There was just so much to attract people. Of course, all we did was play jazz, and good arrangements, and everything. So, I never will forget. But, Wingy and I were living at the Buckhoff Hotel, and, uh, Wingy, I was trying to handle, uh, porch out from the Wingy. And, I never will forget, uh, I saw Wingy got coming out when I pulled up some years. I don't remember what's going on. And, uh, next morning, Wingy was gone. He had caught a train. A freight train. With that one arm, to Chicago. And, uh, he had connections in Chicago. He had always worked in Chicago. And, uh, but, Wingy, just to give you an idea how good this band was, Wingy would hitchhike to Dallas, trying to book this band under its own name. And, of course, the most success I can cause was Dallas at all, the man of band. But, this was a really unusual jazz band for the time. And, uh, so, uh, we, uh, we came back and we couldn't book anything. And, so that, the reason for him to catch the freight train in Chicago, and then all the guys went different directions after that. And, then, we broke up. But, I had a chance to go to the Pumifus concert with, uh, up in England. And, I had a chance to go to Jenkins Music Company and work for my old boss in Oklahoma City. And, uh, Nick, this is the truth. I had, uh, I had a gold con alto sax. And, uh, I hadn't really get to it. I didn't want to call on my first school. So, I hocked my alto sax for ten dollars. And, I caught a bus. And, this is the truth. I caught a bus. At that time, you could ride a bus for a penny a mile. And, it was roughly 400 miles to Oklahoma City from Troop. And, so, uh, I landed in the sweep in, uh, Oklahoma City without a saxophone, but with my friend there and the job is to Jenkins Music Company. And, uh, I think I had to go to my college. And, uh, but I got started wonderfully in, uh, Oklahoma City and played with the very best bands. And, worked in the band department at the daytime, so I was, uh, getting on the plan. And, that's when Bernice and I were married in 1934. But, anyway, that's, this thing can go on and on. Um, I, I, I tell you, the best known name band I played with, I guess, was, uh, Francis Craig's band in Nashville. He played with better bands, but none better known. But, he had, uh, with Luke Needy and all those things. He had a real fine band. He'd been at the Hermitius Hotel for 25 years. So, I, I actually came from Wichita in 1943 to, uh, join John Gordy, where Papa John Gordy made a lot of records. He was, uh, he was a long-time friend of mine. We played together over in Elvira, Arkansas in the 20s, and he had been with Craig 20 years. He really ran the band. Craig just came down, you know, kicked off and wagged the stick, waved the stick. But, uh, anyway, I played with Craig for a time. And, at that time, I was on the camp shows with Minnie Ferrell and I did Pardews and all the present opera stars, the older ones at that time. And, but I didn't mind, really. We played, uh, Sewanee, Castle Heights. We played at the real room of the hotel at noon and for dinner. Then we'd pack up and go and play, uh, maybe Columbia, military school, maybe Sewanee, or just around all that territory. So, I got home to a three-a-ponk and I had been too long, a routine, self-aware. I mean, this didn't suit me very well. So, I decided I'd better get back to New York, so. And, uh, so I went on back to Wichita. Again, the job that I had, I could have caught on, but I didn't, uh, choose to bump another guy off. So, the company transferred me on up to Topeka Canyon, which I was where I was for a year. And then, Armie Brown, who I had met in the thirties with the Herbie Holmes Band, had come back to Jackson, Mississippi. And he and I had become good friends in Wichita. And so, he had organized this music store here in Jackson. And, um, he started corresponding with me when he'd come back. And when he got his store up to the point where he felt like he could afford another person in life, he made me a little girl up. And I came down here and stayed a week to be sure that I could, that I felt like I could fit back into the South. And, uh, so I came here in 1945, and I've been here ever since. So, I guess on that note, that would be a good thing to, a good time to stop boring you with all this history.
Well, I have a few little questions. I'd be glad if you would. Okay. Uh, we covered a lot of territory. Uh, what kind of reeds did Fahs use? You were talking about something? Vandora.

He liked them. He liked them. He, uh, he much preferred the Vandora reeds than anything else. And, uh, when he didn't have, uh, money to buy a box, well, I would pick out the very best reeds in the box for him. And, uh, at that time, uh, Fahs and Sal Franzella were very close. Well, I say friends. They were, uh, Fahs was a great, great jazz musician. And, uh, Sal Franzella was, uh, historically a tremendously well-trained saxophonist in China. He later played with Paul Whiteman. And, uh, New Orleans is full of great stories about, uh, himself. About, uh, uh... Fahsolo? No, not Fahsolo. Uh, this, uh, uh... Well, anyway, he later became a salesman with the Salman Company. He was a former white man. He died in New Orleans a few years ago. He later became a very fine jazz pianist, too, but not. See, there's such a difference in players. Uh-huh. I mean, he could do anything with a horn. Yet, Fahsolo was a much better jazz man. You know, for one thing, the tone was so different. The tone is entirely different, it's true. I don't know if you remember this, but, uh, Fahsolo played the album system, and there is a little tonal difference in the two. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I got to know, well, there were so many good clients in New Orleans during the time I was down there digging. I once marched in a parade. The only parade I ever marched was in the evening, during the Marley Grove, in New Orleans. The same Johnny Brent got me the job, and they had, in this band, they had Azola, they had Nina Pekona, they had Myer Weinberg, who was Gene Meyer, I think he calls himself now. They just had all of the jazz musicians in this parade, and some guys that maybe didn't play very often at all, but they'd pull them out of the Union with getting at least enough to play the Union dues for the year, you know, make it on a parade. But New Orleans was, I tell you, I really enjoyed it, and I learned so much. I got, I'm not a real good friend of Raymond Burke at all. I just know him. But he was playing at the, and I'll take it back, there was another club in the quarter, it was called the Plantation Club. And Ray, Ray Burke was playing there, in 1932. And they had a little Port East Band. And it was, it was quite good. They wanted radio every night. Well, there were just so many good New Orleans musicians, like Bill Pedrona, who you never heard of, but one of the band, great trumpet players. And, excuse me, go ahead.
I want to ask you some technical things, since you sold instruments. Oh, yeah. And reeds and all that. How hard a reed would people use in those days?

Most musicians, Dick, would actually use, most of the good players would use two and a half to three. Some extremists would use four, real hard reeds, but most of the guys would play a two and a half to three. And, to get the right sound, most of them used a medium open lay mouthpiece. Again, some of the guys would use. It depended on how, depended on how, how they wanted to sound. You know, mouthpiece is really, if you have your choice between a good horn and a bad mouthpiece and a good mouthpiece and a bad horn, you better take the mouthpiece. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Red Bowman was with him, Ellis Stratikas, the trombonist from Galaxia was with him, and no one was a friend of mine. They were around the store all the time, and that's how I got to know, so I was talking on the other hand. But I played with little bands like that. You know a guy, a butcher, like Joe Clancy, he booked jobs, he was a drummer, and he, I played with him, and the piano player, we sometimes used to play for bingo parties, all kind of things. At that time, they had to have music for nearly everything. Go ahead and ask me some of them.

Well Joe Clancy is famous, the stories about him. Yeah. Francis Murray, who you probably don't remember, he was a young man, and a saxophone player where he used to play stories about Joe Clancy. Well anyway, was there any special sort of ligature you used to, or that people generally use since you worked in the store?

Ligatures, most all of them are made in France, and there are different names put on them. The banal, the O-N-A-B-E, is what I actually used. But there are so many different variations of them. I just recently sent one that I got to put Brown in the water. And, Bud, I knew in St. Louis, his brother lives here in town. And he, I had this patented special ligature made by Gigliotti, he's a famous plant editor, and it was good, but I didn't find a big picture of the difference. It was made of plastic, and I had a certain image. I just sent it to Bud with the hope that maybe he could use it. He's experimenting around all the time.
I've even seen people pass string around there. Were you to believe in that?
The old theater clarinists back there, they used to take Fred. Yeah, Black Fred. And, and that was, now that's a purist for you.
Yeah. And, what kind of mouthpieces did you all use?

Oh, well, I, of course I always, I used a Selmer Table D, hard rubber mouthpiece for a long period of years. I hadn't become that technical until I got to where I really was interested in learning how to play. But, I then got a Dix to Beal back by 1935. Dix to Beal is in New Orleans, now director of the office at the World War was a hotel. But, anyhow, he had, he was very popular with Ben Burney at this time. And, so the wood-winning people put out this Dix to Beal special. I used that thing for 25 years. I was crazy. And, I dropped it from my office one day and broke it. And, so what I'm using now is Mitchell LeRae. And, Mitchell LeRae is a famous kind of teacher in California. That's the kind of reads I use now. And, Doran's became so unreliable that you'd have to buy a box to get one or two. Incidentally, with our good friend, Pinasako, he still doesn't, he'll buy a box to get one out of it. But, that's the, that's the one you've seen over there.
That's, he's one of my all time favorites. Very favorite one. And, to go on down the horn itself. Yeah. What kind of, what kind of horn do you prefer? Or, did the people use there generally?

Always. Now, Faso actually played the Pinsley Mule. Uh-huh. And, Sal Franzela played the song. Al Galladera played the song. All the, all the mouthfeeds and the saxophone. But, traditionally, woodwind people always have preferred either LeBlanc, LeBay, Salmer. Pinsley Mule was an extremely popular American made clarinet, made in New York. But, most of the clarinets always traditionally have been made in France. The best ones, there were German clarinets, and still are, they still make the album system. But, the French clarinets, they have it, I mean, they, all of the LeBlanc clarinets are made in France. And, all of the Salmer clarinets, with the real Salmer name on the Hermadian patch. But, all men, there are hundreds of different names of clarinets that I could rattle off to. But, you're speaking with great professionals. Most of them have used Salmer, LeBlanc, or LeBay. And, then, you have some of them.

Something else I remember reading about it, maybe you can talk to Jack, that was Doc Ross's band, when they called it the Cowboy Band, in Los Angeles. Yeah. Did you all have to wear any outfits or anything to look like that?

I did. When I joined the Doc Ross Band in California in 1925, they were playing at Solomon's Penny Danstree Lodge. This was an unbelievable place. Huge ballroom. Paid a penny a dance. They had three bands. One was Ranger Ross, Texas Cowboy Band, direct from Texas. And, then, we played the popular music. We played the popular music. Mosby's Dixieland Blue Bloys with a black band, which was fabulous, looking back. I mean, Jack and I used to go over and stand by the stand, the bandstand, just to get to hear them. Then, they had a band of all nations called Godderson's Band of All Nations. This was composed of an American freshman, supposedly, and California, true California style. But, back to the uniforms, Doc had bought these expensive tailor-made chaps, complete cowboy outfits. And, they went out to Pasadena and corked the train. And, I have a picture of the band with Jack playing his trombone on the cowcatcher of the engine. And, I mean, that's the way they were promoting things in California, even that far back. They had horses in front of this Penny Dance Deluxe, Solomon's Penny Dance Deluxe. And, they were out in front of the place. And, they had a lobby. It was all done with the leather companies there in town. They had all beautiful saddles and everything for horseback riding in the lobby of this place. They had free lunch at the Spalding. Now, this is no. Spalding, that's good. Anyway, that's where the Ranger Ross was. The band's name was really Doc Ross Jazz Bandits, B-A-N-G-I-T-S. Doc was from Indiana. But, he'd gotten down into Texas. And, for years, he was one of the most popular bands in Texas. He played at the Lake Wichita Dance Pavilion in the summers, and they booked all around that, part of Texas in the wintertime. But, see, Jack would go back. Whenever he got out of a job, he knew he could always go back to Doc Ross. So, no matter where he'd go, he'd come back and play Doc Ross. He'd go out a lot of time. But, he also had another wonderful trombone player, Red Stewart. He and Jack alternated between the years. When Jack would come, Red would leave. Jack would leave, Red would come back. So, this is interesting too.
Well, did they, did you, were you on that famous parade? When the horseback?

No. I had gotten in just the day before. And, I followed behind the parade in the Dodge 4 with my wife and her aunt. But, they, they did parade. They did parade. On the horses. And, it was a sight to behold, I'm telling you. All these musicians, some of them could ride, some of them couldn't. But, anyway. Fantastic. They went out to the Biltmore Hotel. And, hitched the horses. How many? And, it was about 90's bands. Big band for those days. They had a lot of, I have pictures, I want you to see them. So, if you have time. Well. But, that was, that was some kind of a historic band. They had a guy named Walter Botts, who had been with Doc for years. And, he was a very handsome guy. He was a wonderful, C Melody sax player. Well. When I.

segments.title: Opening: name, place and library collection
segments.summary: Kelly gives his name (E.T. Kelly, Edward Timothy) and the Jackson, Mississippi address; the interviewer explains the library collection.

segments.title: Birth in Mississippi, family from Marshall, Texas
segments.summary: Born July 25, 1905 in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, to a Tex-Pacific railroad family living in Marshall, Texas.

segments.title: Family music and the first clarinet
segments.summary: Sisters played piano, an uncle was a country fiddler; Kelly learned from records and a neighbor boy, and bought an Albert System clarinet for $36.

segments.title: First paid jobs and leaving home to join Ham Crawford
segments.summary: He plays C-melody sax for $12.50, plays with small bands around Texas, runs off without permission, and joins Ham Crawford's band at sixteen.

segments.title: Ham Crawford, Jack Gardner's orchestra and Wingy Manone
segments.summary: Ham Crawford's background and the famous Jack Gardner orchestra; talk of Wingy Manone and the Doc Ross band.

segments.title: Buddy's Blue Melody Boys and Jack Teagarden's first Shreveport trio
segments.summary: After Lake Charles in 1923 Kelly helps form the Blue Melody Boys, touring by Ford and booked by Jasper Tompkins; Teagarden first plays Shreveport with a trio.

segments.title: Houston, Wichita Falls, the Louisiana Ramblers, California and Werlein's
segments.summary: One long account of offers by telegram, the Louisiana Ramblers, going to California with Teagarden and Doc Ross, and choosing the music store business around 1926.

segments.title: Tape adjustment and reminder about New Orleans
segments.summary: The interviewer says Kelly has not talked about New Orleans; short pause to turn the machine.

segments.title: Heading to New Orleans in 1932: Ben Pollack band and Bourbon Street
segments.summary: Kelly recounts the Depression, hearing the Ben Pollack band, the Studio Club and Silver Slipper, and getting a job offer with Mr. LaCoste.

segments.title: Arriving in New Orleans and living on Bourbon Street
segments.summary: Kelly drives to New Orleans with the Nurse brothers and shares a room with drummer Johnny Grant.

segments.title: Booking jobs in front of Werlein's and the Presidents' Ball
segments.summary: Musicians book spot jobs at Werlein's counter; Kelly plays with Gimelli and Pete Lesseps, explains the Presidents' Ball, and becomes assistant manager.

segments.title: Life in the French Quarter, then Dick Richardson's band, Craig and Jackson
segments.summary: Roommate life with Snoozer Quinn visiting, losing the Werlein job, the Dick Richardson band and Wingy, Oklahoma City, Francis Craig in Nashville, and settling in Jackson in 1945.

segments.title: Fazola, Sal Franzella and New Orleans clarinetists
segments.summary: Reed preferences of Fazola, comparison with Sal Franzella, a Mardi Gras parade band and Raymond Burke at the Plantation Club.

segments.title: Reed strength and mouthpieces, and small-time New Orleans jobs
segments.summary: Good players used reeds of 2.5 to 3 with a medium open mouthpiece; Kelly mentions bingo-party jobs with Joe Clancy.

segments.title: Ligatures and the mouthpieces Kelly used
segments.summary: Ligatures are mostly French; Kelly describes his Selmer mouthpieces, the Dixie-Beal special and string ligatures.

segments.title: Clarinet makes and the Albert and Boehm systems
segments.summary: Fazola played Penzel-Mueller; woodwind players prefer Leblanc, Selmer or Buffet, mostly French made.

segments.title: Doc Ross's Cowboy band at Solomon's Penny Dance in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Kelly joins Doc Ross's Jazz Bandits in California in 1925, with Jack Teagarden and Red Stewart, cowboy outfits, and the horseback parade.
